name: Lecture Note: Cranial Cavity
text: Page 1 of 9 Cranial cavity ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Know the overall structure of the skull and define the different bones bounding the cranial cavity. 2. Describe the different layers of the meninges and their related spaces with their clinical significance. 3. Describe the dural folds dividing the cranial cavity. 4. Differentiate between the dural venous sinuses regarding their site and termination. 5. Relate some clinical conditions to their anatomical basis. CLINICAL PROBLEM A patient came to the ER complaining of sever headache, diplopia, redness and swelling of one eye. He told the physician that few days ago, he had a boil in the upper lip that became inflamed and septic. What is the most probable diagnosis? - Cranial cavity : The cranial cavity lodges the brain and its coverings, cranial nerves and supplying vessels. Its floor is divided into anterior, middle, and posterior cranial fossae. (Fig. 1) Figure 1. Cranial cavity. - Anterior cranial fossa : (Fig. 2) The anterior cranial fossa lies above the nasal cavity and the two orbits. The frontal bone shows the frontal crest with foramen cecum behind the crest. The floor of the anterior cranial fossa is formed of : 1- Anteriorly : the cribriform plate of ethmoid bone that presents the crista galli and on each side, the orbital plate of the frontal bone. 2- Posteriorly : the body of sphenoid and the lesser wing of the sphenoid on each side. The lesser wing ends as the anterior clinoid process and the optic canal lies medial to the process. Page 2 of 9 The cribriform plate of ethmoid and body of sphenoid roof the nasal cavity while the orbital plate of frontal bone and lesser wing of sphenoid roof the orbit. Figure 2. (A) anterior cranial fossa. (B) anterior view of skull - Middle cranial fossa : (Fig. 3) The floor of the middle cranial fossa is formed by the body of the sphenoid in the middle with the greater wing of the sphenoid and the squamous part of temporal bone on each side. Sella turcica The body of sphenoid shows the sella turcica which is composed of : 1- hypophyseal fossa that lodges the pituitary gland. 2- tuberculum sellae that forms the anterior wall of the sella turcica. 3- dorsum sellae that forms the posterior wall of the sella turcica. Its upper border shows the posterior clinoid processes. The middle cranial fossa shows the following foramina arranged from before backwards : superior orbital fissure, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum. At the apex of the petrous part of temporal bone, foramen lacerum lies. A B Figure 3. Middle cranial fossa. Page 3 of 9 - Posterior cranial fossa : (Fig. 4) It contains the brainstem (midbrain, pons, and medulla) and the cerebellum. Anteriorly, it is bounded by the dorsum sellae and the clivus that slopes downwards till foramen magnum. Posteriorly, the occipital bone shows the internal occipital protuberance with the internal occipital crest extending downwards. On each side of the protuberance, the transverse sulcus extends and continues as the sigmoid sulcus that ends at the jugular foramen. Above the jugular foramen, lies the internal acoustic meatus while below the foramen, the hypoglossal canal is present. Figure 4. posterior cranial fossa. - Meninges : (Fig. 5) The brain, as well as the spinal cord, is surrounded by three layers of membranes (meninges) : - an outer layer; the dura mater. - a middle layer; the arachnoid mater. - an inner layer; the pia mater. 1- Dura mater : (Fig. 5,6) It is the tough outer covering of the brain in close contact with the arachnoid mater. Figure 5. Meninges. dorsum sellae Page 4 of 9 - Dural folds (partitions) : They project into the cranial cavity and partially subdivide it into compartments for the parts of the brain. They include the falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli, falx cerebelli, and diaphragma sellae. Figure 6 (A&B). Dural folds and spaces of the meninges. 1- Falx cerebri : (Fig. 6,7) It is a sickle-shaped fold between the two cerebral hemispheres. It is attached anteriorly to the crista galli and frontal crest. Posteriorly it is attached to the tentorium cerebelli. 2- Falx cerebelli : (Fig. 6,7) It is a midline fold attached posteriorly to the internal occipital crest and superiorly to the tentorium cerebelli. Its anterior edge lies between the two cerebellar hemispheres. Figure 7 (A&B). Dural folds. 3- Diaphragma sellae : (Fig. 6,7) It is attached to the anterior and posterior clinoid processes overlying the pituitary gland. It is pierced by the infundibulum, connecting the pituitary gland with the hypothalamus. A B A B Page 5 of 9 4- Tentorium cerebelli : (Fig. 7,8) It is a tent-shaped fold that separates the cerebellum in the posterior cranial fossa from the cerebral hemispheres. It has an outer border attached to the internal occipital protuberance, transverse sulci, upper borders of the petrous parts of temporal bones, dorsum sellae and the posterior clinoid processes. Its inner border is free attached anteriorly to the anterior clinoid processes bounding an opening (tentorial notch), through which the midbrain passes. 2- Arachnoid mater : (Fig. 5,6) It lines the inner layer of the dura mater. It does not follow the grooves of the brain, except for the longitudinal fissure between the two cerebral hemispheres. 3- Pia mater : (Fig. 5,6) It closely invests the surface of the brain. It follows the grooves of the brain, and is closely applied to the cranial nerves at their origins. - Extradural (epidural) space is a potential space between the dura and the bones of skull. (Fig. 6) - Subdural space is a potential subdural space between the dura and arachnoid. (Fig. 6) - Subarachnoid space lies between the arachnoid mater and pia mater. It contains cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and the brain blood vessels. (Fig. 6) - Clinical notes : - Trauma may result in bleeding into the extradural space giving extradural hematoma. - Subarachnoid hemorrhage : may occur due to cerebral trauma or from a ruptured aneurysm of a blood vessel supplying the brain. - Dural venous sinuses : Veins draining the brain empty into dural venous sinuses that eventually lead to the internal jugular veins. The dural venous sinuses receive also emissary veins which connect extracranial veins to the dural venous sinuses. The sinuses may be single or paired. Figure 8. Tentorium cerebelli. Page 6 of 9 Single sinuses Paired sinuses Superior sagittal. Spheno-parietal sinuses. Inferior sagittal. Cavernous sinuses. Straight sinus. Superior petrosal sinuses. Occipital sinus. Inferior petrosal sinuses. Intercavernous sinuses. Transverse sinuses. Sigmoid sinuses. 1- Superior sagittal sinus : (Fig. 6,7,9,10) It lies in the upper border of the falx cerebri. It begins anteriorly at foramen cecum, where it may receive an emissary vein from the nasal cavity, and ends posteriorly at the internal occipital protuberance where it continues as the right transverse sinus. Figure 9 (A&B). Dural venous sinuses. 2- Inferior sagittal sinus : (Fig. 6,7,9,10) It lies in the lower border of the falx cerebri. Posteriorly, it is joined by the great cerebral vein to form the straight sinus. 3- Straight sinus : (Fig. 6,7,9,10) It passes posteriorly along the junction of the falx cerebri and the tentorium cerebelli to the internal occipital protuberance where it continues as the left transverse sinus. 4- Transverse sinus : (Fig. 9,10) It lies in the transverse sulcus along the attached margin of the tentorium cerebelli and continues as the sigmoid sinus. The right transverse sinus (a continuation of the superior sagittal sinus) is larger in size than the left (a continuation of the smaller straight sinus). A B Page 7 of 9 5- Sigmoid sinus : (Fig. 9,10) It lies in the sigmoid sulcus that extends to the jugular foramen where it continues as the internal jugular vein. 6- Occipital sinus : (Fig. 6,10) It lies along the attached margin of the falx cerebelli. 7- Spheno-parietal sinus : (Fig. 10) It runs along the lesser wing of sphenoid to end in the cavernous sinus. 8- Cavernous sinus : - Site : lateral side of the body of the sphenoid on either side of the sella turcica. (Fig. 9) - Tributaries : The cavernous sinus receives blood from : (Fig. 10) a. cerebral veins. b. spheno-parietal sinus. c. veins of the orbit. d. veins from the face. Figure 10. Dural venous sinuses. - Drainage : by the superior and inferior petrosal sinuses. (Fig. 9,10) - Connections : it is connected with : a. the orbit. b. the face. c. opposite cavernous sinus by intercavenous sinuses around the infundibulum. Therefore, extracranial infections may pass to the cranial cavity through these connections. - Structures that pass through the cavernous sinus : (Fig. 11) 1- internal carotid artery. 2- abducent (6th cranial) nerve. - Structures in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus : (Fig. 11) 1- oculomotor (3rd cranial) nerve. 2- trochlear (4th cranial) nerve. 3- ophthalmic nerve (branch of the 5th cranial nerve). 4- maxillary nerve (branch of the 5th cranial nerve). Page 8 of 9 Figure 11. Cavernous sinus. 9- Superior petrosal sinus : (Fig. 9,10) It begins at the posterior end of the cavernous sinus, runs along the upper border of the petrous part of temporal bone in the attached border of tentorium cerebelli to end in the transverse sinus. 10- Inferior petrosal sinus : (Fig. 9,10) It begins at the posterior end of the cavernous sinus, runs along the lower border of the petrous part of temporal bone and passes through the jugular foramen to end in the internal jugular vein. - Clinical notes : - Meningitis: infection of the meninges. The patient may have headache, fever, drowsiness and stiff neck. - Emissary veins connect extracranial veins with intracranial sinuses and are important clinically because they may transmit extracranial infections to the cranial cavity as they have no valves. - Cavernous sinus thrombosis : (Fig. 12) It may cause severe headache, diplopia, redness and swelling of the eye. It may result from an infection of the eye or the face transmitted to the cavernous sinus. Figure 12. Cavernous sinus thrombosis.

name: Lecture Note: Posterior Triangle
text: Page 1 of 4 L 5 Anatomy of the Posterior triangle of the neck ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Appraise the importance of sternocleidomastoid muscle for identifying the different structures of the neck. 2. Differentiate between the different layers of the fascia of the neck. 3. Differentiate between different boundaries of the posterior triangle. 4. Appraise the structures forming the roof and the floor of the posterior triangle. 5. Correlate the boundaries & contents of the posterior triangl e to their clinical importance. Sternocleidomastoid (Sternomastoid) muscle: • The sternocleidomastoid muscle divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles, • When it contracts, it appears as an oblique band crossing the side of the neck from the sternoclavicular joint to the mastoid process of the skull. (fig. 1) Origin: Anterior surface of the sternum and medial one- third of the clavicle. Insertion: Lateral surface of the mastoid process of the skull. Nerve supply: Spinal Accessory nerve [XI] Actions: Individually it will: • Tilt the head toward the shoulder on the same side (i.e., lateral flexion of the neck) • Rotating head to turn the face superiorly to the opposite side. Acting together, both muscles will draw the head forward (i.e., anterior flexion of the neck). Clinical Correlates: - Torticollis: it means spasm of the sternomastoid muscle, which is a painful condition and leads to abnormal head posture. - The carotid pulse is palpated along the anterior border of the sternomastoid muscle. Figure 1: sternomastoid muscle Page 2 of 4 Deep fascia of the neck There are two fasciae in the neck – the superficial cervical fascia and the deep cervical fascia. Platysma muscle: - It is a broad thin superficial muscle which lies anteriorly in the neck in the superficial cervical fascia. (fig. 2) - Innervation: facial nerve Deep Cervical Fascia: The deep cervical fascia is organized into several layers: (fig. 3) 1. Investing Layer: It surrounds all the structures in the neck. It divides where it meets the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles and surrounds them. 2. Pretracheal Layer: It is situated in the anterior neck. Thyroid gland and infrahyoid muscles are enclosed by the pretracheal fascia. 3. Prevertebral Layer: The prevertebral fascia surrounds the vertebral column and its associated muscles. 4. Carotid Sheath: It encloses the neurovascular bundle of the neck. Clinical Correlates: The thyroid gland and all thyroid swellings move with the swallowing/deglutition because the pretracheal fascia surrounds the gland. Figure 2: Platysma muscle Figure 3: Layers of the deep cervical fascia Page 3 of 4 The posterior triangle of the neck The posterior triangle of the neck is on the lateral aspect of the neck posterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle. (fig.4) Boundaries of the posterior triangle: (fig.4,5) Anteriorly: the sternomastoid muscle. Posteriorly: the trapezius muscle. Apex: the occipital bone where attachments of trapezius & sternomastoid come together. Base: the middle one third of the clavicle. Roof of the posterior triangle: 1. Skin, 2. Superficial fascia of the neck, 3. Deep fascia including the investing layer of the cervical fascia that surrounds the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius muscles as it passes through the region. Floor of the posterior triangle: It is formed by a muscular floor covered by a fascia: (fig.5) 1. Prevertebral layer of the cervical fascia. 2. Muscles from superior to inferior: • Splenius capitis, • Levator scapulae, • Scalene muscles. Contents of the posterior triangle: (fig.6) Muscle: inferior belly of omohyoid muscle. Nerves: • Spinal accessory nerve, • Posterior branches from the cervical plexus of nerves, • Trunks of the brachial plexus. Vessels: • External jugular vein, • Subclavian artery (3rd part) and some branches, • Subclavian vein. Figure 4: posterior triangle of the neck Figure 5: boundaries and floor of the posterior triangle of the neck Figure 6: contents of the posterior triangle of the neck Page 4 of 4 Clinical Correlates: - Injury to the spinal accessory nerve (e.g. due to trauma in the posterior triangle) can result in paralysis of the trapezius muscle.

name: Lecture PPT: Development of Head & Neck
text: Development of Head & Neck Nehal Mohamed Nabil Assist. Professor of Anatomy & Embryology Dear students & Transfer Goal To appreciate the stages of Head& Neck development , and the related clinical conditions. Students’ learning outcomes At the end of this session, the student should be able to: Interpret the development & structure of branchial apparatus. Differentiate between the derivatives of the branchial arches. Correlate the nerve supply of different head& neck structures to their development. Appraise the congenital anomalies affecting the head & neck relative to their development. BRANCHIAL (PHARYNGEAL) APPARATUS CLINICAL PROBLEM A patient presents with an abnormal opening on the side of the neck. What might this opening be, and what is its basis embryologically? The branchial arches are six arches, which develop in successive manner from above downward around the pharynx. Each arch contains: a cartilaginous component, a cranial nerve, an artery, and a muscular component. (A) Embryo showing the pharyngeal arches from outside. (B) & (C) Coronal section in the pharynx of an embryo. A B C Branchial Arches The artery supplying the fifth arch degenerates early, so the 5th arch itself degenerates too. 1st arch divides into small maxillary and large mandibular parts. Skeletal derivatives of pharyngeal arches Definitive structures formed by the cartilaginous components of the various pharyngeal arches Definitive structures formed by the cartilaginous components of the various pharyngeal arches (skeletal derivatives) Skeletal derivatives of pharyngeal arches (cont.) Some of the components ossify; others disappear or become ligamentous. The maxillary process and Meckel’s cartilage of the first arch are replaced by the maxilla and mandible, respectively, which develop by membranous ossification. The cartilage of the 2nd arch is called Reichert's cartilage. Fate of the pharyngeal arch cartilages. Endodermal derivatives of the pharyngeal pouches 1st Pharyngeal Pouch: Primitive tympanic cavity& auditory tube 2 nd Pharyngeal Pouch: Palatine tonsil 3rd Pharyngeal Pouch: Forms 2 diverticula: dorsal and ventral. Endoderm of dorsal diverticulum: becomes the inf. Parathyroid gland. Endoderm of ventral diverticulum: becomes the thymus. 4th Pharyngeal Pouch: Also develops dorsal and ventral diverticula. The dorsal bud becomes the Sup. Parathyroid. The ventral bud becomes the Ultimobranchial body. The ultimobranchial body fuses with the thyroid gland and disseminates within it to give the parafollicular C cells which produce calcitonin. Endodermal derivatives of the pharyngeal pouches (cont.) The first cleft penetrates the underlying mesoderm to form the external auditory meatus. The mesoderm of the second arch proliferates to form the operculum. This operculum grows caudally to overlap the third and fourth clefts. The operculum forms a space between it and the clefts called cervical sinus. This sinus will disappear to give smooth contour of the neck. Ectodermal derivatives of pharyngeal clefts Abnormalities of Branchial Arches Ectopic thymus and parathyroid. Branchial fistulas : Occurs when pharyngeal pouch 2 and pharyngeal groove 2 persist, thereby forming a patent opening from the internal tonsillar area to the external neck. It is generally found along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. 3. Branchial (cervical) cyst: Occurs when parts of the pharyngeal grooves 2, 3, and 4 that are normally obliterated persist, thereby forming a cyst. Cervical Cyst “Branchial Cyst” CLINICAL PROBLEM Branchial fistula Development of the face The face is developed from five processes: The maxillary processes (2 in number, originated from the first branchial arch). 2. The mandibular processes (one on each side, originated from the first branchial arch). 3. Frontonasal process formed by proliferation of the mesoderm ventral to the brain. The ectoderm on both sides of the frontonasal process will form nasal placode. The nasal placode invaginates the underlying structures& will transform into nasal pit. Development of the face (cont.) The nasal pits divide the frontonasal process into lateral & medial nasal processes. The frontonasal process will form the bridge of the nose; the medial nasal processes will form the tip of nose and the filtrum of upper lip, while the lateral nasal processes will form the alae of the nose. The nasal pits excavated to form the nasal cavities. Development of the face (cont.) The maxillary processes increase in size and grow medially. They meet the medial nasal processes; compress them towards the mid line. Finally the maxillary process fuses with the medial nasal process. The maxillary process will form the upper lip. Development of the face (cont.) The lateral nasal process and the maxillary process are separated by deep groove called (nasolacrimal groove). Canalization of this groove leads to formation of nasolacrimal duct. The ectoderm of the maxillary processes and the lateral nasal processes will fuse together burring the nasolacrimal duct. This fusion leads to the formation of the upper part of the cheek and the maxilla. Development of the face (cont.) Fusion of the maxillary and mandibular processes leads to formation of the lower part of the cheek. The two mandibular processes grow medially meet and fuse to form the lower lip and lower jaw. Development of the face (cont.) Nerve supply of the processes: Frontonasal process : Ophthalmic nerve. 2. Maxillary processes: Maxillary nerve. 3. Mandibular processes :Mandibular nerve. Abnormalities of the face: 1. Cleft upper lip (hare lip): Most common congenital anomaly, It is due to failure of fusion of the maxillary process and the medial nasal process. 2. Oblique facial cleft: Defect in the face extends from the medial angle of eye to upper lip. It is due to failure of fusion of lateral nasal process with the maxillary process .The nasolacrimal duct is exposed to the surface. 3. Median cleft lower lip It is a rare anomaly. It is due to failure of fusion of the 2 mandibular processes. Summary Understanding the developmental process of head& neck structures is essential for the proper diagnosis and management of their congenital malformations. Abnormal facial features indicates abnormal development of pharyngeal arches. Sadler, T. W., & Langman, J. (2012). Langman's medical embryology (13th ed.). name: PPT- Structure of the skin & sensory nerve endings
text: L 9 Histology of the skin & sensory nerve endings Dr Rehab Ahmed Abdel-Moneim Professor of histology & cell biology 1.Differentiate between microstructure of the skin layers 2. Classify sensory nerve endings on histological basis. 3. Correlate structure & site of different skin sensory nerve endings to their specific function. 4. Correlate microstructure of the muscle spindle & Golgi tendon organs to their functions. At the end of this lecture, the students should be able to: Integumentary System 1- The skin I- The Epidermis II- The Dermis 2- Skin appendages: A- Hair. B. Nail. C. Sebaceous glands. D. Sweat glands. I- The epidermis Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium II- The Dermis Loose areolar & dense irregular CT Types of skin: I- Thin skin II- Thick skin; palm of hands & & sole of feet Layers of the Skin Dermis The epidermis The epithelium is composed of 4 types of cells I- Keratinocytes; cells synthesize intermediate filaments keratin. II- Non-keratinocytes (no keratin synthesis) Melanocytes Langerhans’ cells Merkel cells I- Keratinocytes: 5 Layers SL A- Keratinocytes: 5 strata desquamating cells Process of keratinization►►takes 15-30 days ►►desquamation of the horny layer Deduce structural features of each layer in relation to its function 1-Stratum basal; high rate of mitosis & responsible for renewal of other cell layers. 2- Stratum spinosum; thickest layer, polyhedral cells still undergo mitosis. Keratin synthesis increases. Cells are interconnected by desmosomes (mechanical stability). Cells contain lamellated granules. 3-Stratum granulosum; Flat cells that contain keratohyaline granules (packing of keratin filaments) and lamellar bodies (exocytosis of contents to form sheets of lipid rich material; (water-proof barrier). 4- Stratum Lucidum Only in thick skin. Cells lack organelles & nuclei; contain only keratin. 5- Stratum Corneum Flat dead cells that contain keratin only. Undergoes desquamation. Non capable of keratin synthesis. Not attached to keratinocytes. 1- Melanocytes 2- Langerhans’ cells 3- Merkel cells Non-Keratinocytes 1- MELANOCYTES Site: In st. basale Function: Synthesis of melanin pigment. Melanin granules are injected into surrounding keratinocytes Between cell of stratum spinosum Multiple processes that extend to St granulosum. Motile cell Function Antigen presenting Role in hypersensitivity reactions 2-Langerhan cells 3- MERKEL CELLS In basal layer Large Attached to keratinocytes Function Sensory receptor to light touch. Slow adapting The dermis & hypodermis The junction between dermis & epidermis is corrugated; dermal papillae (elevations) that interdigitate with epidermal ridges. (WHY?) To increase surface area of contact for better epidermal nourishment. What are the types of tissue in the dermis? Papillary layer; superficial loose areolar tissue. Reticular layer: deeper layer formed of dense irregular CT interlacing with elastic fibers. NB; The hypodermis is not part of the skin & formed of adipose CT. Thick Skin Dermal papillae St Lucidum Types of skin Thick skin Thin Skin Epidermal Thickness Thick Thin Site Palms and soles The rest of the body Stratum corneum Much thicker Much thinner Dermo-epidermal interdigitations Regular, deep and more numerous Irregular, shallow and less numerous Sweat glands More numerous Less numerous Hair follicles and sebaceous glands Absent Present What is a receptor? It is the specialized sensory nerve ending of a sensory nerve fiber. Each type of sensory nerve ending has a special structure and pattern at its termination in a specific site (skin or muscle). Classification of sensory receptors Functionally Mechanoreceptors, Ex; Pacinian’s corpuscles, Meissner’s corpuscle, muscle spindle & Golgi tendon organs. Thermoreceptors Nociceptors (pain) Others rods & cones in the retina, gustatory cells in the taste bud & olfactory epithelium in the nose. What is the result of receptor stimulation? Generation of action potential along the sensory axon. Chemoreceptors Olfactory cells Gustatory cells Olfactory epithelium Taste Buds Structurally: 1- Encapsulated; covered by a CT capsule 2- Non encapsulated; free nerve endings, Merkel’s disks Type A- Merkel’s disk B- Meissner C- Pacinian Site Stratum basale Dermal papillae Deep in dermis & hypodermis Structure (axon loses its myelin sheath at the end) Ends by flat expanded part in contact with Merkel’s cell Axon has a spiral course between Schwann cells Axon has an axial course, ends by a terminal bulb. Concentric collagen fibers, Schwann cells & fibroblasts Function Slow adapting to light pressure & touch Fine Touch (velocity) Vibrations, deep pressure 20 Pacinian & Meissner’s corpuscles Pacinian Meissner’s D- Free nerve endings; pain & temperature. Mixed receptors; chemical, mechanical or thermal. 1- Pain nerve endings; penetrate the basal lamina, ramify(branches) in between the epidermis cells till granular cells layer (WHY?) To spread over a wide surface area to perceive pain more efficiently. 2- Thermoreceptors; penetrate the basal lamina & also gives branches parallel to the dermal epidermal junction. Pathway of sensations transmitted from skin receptors 1- Sensory receptor Action potential is generated in the axon hillock close to the sensory nerve ending 2- Pseudounipolar neurons central process synapses with sensory neurons in the spinal cord 1 2 3 Site Muscle spindle Golgi tendon organs Between skeletal muscle fibers near the tendon At junction between tendon & muscle Core Intrafusal muscle fibers Collagen fibers Function& Innervation Stretch receptor; monitors degree of muscle stretch (length) & induces reflex contraction Tension receptor; monitors force of contraction Encapsulated mechanoreceptors in the skeletal muscle 1- Muscle spindle 2- Golgi tendon organs 1- Structure of the muscle spindle 1- CT capsule; separating it from the skeletal muscle fibers (extra fusal fibers) 2- Content; intrafusal fibers of two types: A- Nuclear chain; cylindrical, uniform, nuclei are arranged in one row B- Nuclear bag (dynamic & static); swollen middle part that contains randomly oriented nuclei Both types lack myofibrils at their central (non contractile central parts) Peripheral portions contain myofibrils and are contractile 25 3- Innervation of the muscle spindle Gamma efferent Motor axons to peripheral zones of intrafusal fibers; to maintain them stretched and sensitive. Primary (Ia) afferent sensory axons that end by annulo spiral endings on all types of intra fusal fibers. Secondary II afferent sensory axons that end by flower spray endings on static type of nuclear bag fibers & nuclear chain Functional variation: Group Ia and group II fibers both respond to a stretching of the muscle at a constant rate. Only group Ia fibers, however, respond to a change in the rate of stretching. a b c 2- Golgi tendon organs Site: junction between tendon & muscle. Structure; ,CT capsule, wavy collagen fibers (role of collagen). Innervation: sensory afferent axons only. To sum up Keratinocytes are represented in 4-5 stages with structural differences. Sensory nerve endings are distributed mostly in the skin. Muscle spindle & Golgi TO are sensory nerve endings related to the skeletal muscle Lecture notes part I & part II. Lecture PPT. text: L17: Histological Features of Cerebral Cortex The cerebrum is made up of the two cerebral hemispheres . Each hemisphere consists of a convoluted cortex of grey matter (the cerebral cortex) overlying the central medullary mass of white matter. In humans, the surface of the cerebral cortex folds to create gyri (ridges) and sulci (furrows) which increase the surface area . The white matter of the cerebral hemispheres contains collection of nerve cells called the basal ganglia. The cerebral cortex has a unique histological structure in order to be able to p erform higher functions. Cytoarchitecture of cerebral cortex 1. Cell bodies of neurons, which are arranged in horizontally -disposed layers (laminae). 2. Different types of neuroglia cells e.g. astrocytes. 3. Blood capillaries. 4. The neuropil (pilus = felt = meshwork); amorphous pale areas formed of:- a. Cell bodies and processes of astrocytes with the processes of neurons forming a tangled network. b. Intercellular spaces containing tissue fluid. This arrangement permits diffusion between capillarie s and neurons which are very sensitive to changes of oxygen and blood sugar level. Neurons of the cerebral cortex: The cerebral cortex consists of the hundreds of billions of neurons, and all of them are different variations of only three morphological shapes: pyramidal cells, fusiform cells and stellate (granular cells). Other types of cells seen in the cortex are a modification one of those three. The other cells are horizontal cells of Cajal and cells of Martinotti. 1. Pyramidal cells: make up to 75% of the cellular component of the cortex and they are the main output neurons of the cerebral cortex. They vary in size, going from small to gigantic. They usually have one thick apical dendrite that courses towards the surface of the cortex, and multiple basal dendrites. They have one long axon arises from the middle of the base that leaves the cortex and enters the subcortical white matter. 2. Stellate (granular) cells: the name granule cells came from the fact that these cells are small and densely -packed giving a granular appearance. They have numerous branching dendrites and a single short axon which may ascend to the cortical surface or descend to the underlying layers. Granule cells are present in all cortical laminae. 3. Fusiform cells: are usually placed in the deepest cortical layer. Their dendrite projects towards the cortical surface, whereas the axon project to the thalamus. 4. Horizontal cells of Cajal: are small, spindle-shaped cells and oriented parallel to the surface only seen in the most superficial part of the cortex. They have one axon and one dendrite, both of them synapsing locally within the most superficial layer. 5. Cells of Martinotti : are multipolar neurons that are most densely located within the deepest layer of the cortex. Their numerous axons and dendrites course towards the surface of the cortex. Layers of the cerebral cortex: The neurons of the cerebral cortex have a laminar alignment. That means that neurons are organized in layers, or laminas, parallel to the surface of the brain, and layers are differentiated between each other by the size and shape of the neuronal bodies. In a typical histological section of the motor area, six layers can be identified arranged from surface inwards as follows: I. The molecular layer (plexiform layer): This is the most superficial layer, lying directly under the pia mater of the the meninges. This layer is very poor with cellular component, which is represented by only a few horizontal cells of Cajal. The major portion of this layer is actually the processes of the neurons lying within the deeper layers and their synapses. II. The external granular layer: This layer consists mostly of stellate cells. The existence of these small cells in this layer gives that “granular” appearance to this layer, hence its name. III. The external pyramidal cell layer: it contains small & medium-sized pyramidal cells which increase in size and decrease in number in the deeper parts of this layer. IV. The internal granular layer: Consists mostly of stellate cells similar to layer II. V. The internal pyramidal cell layer (ganglionic layer): It contains medium -sized & large -sized pyramidal cells. The most important feature of the motor area is its content of giant pyramidal cells (Betz cells). Betz cells constitute the projection neurons of the motor cortex. They are the upper motor neurons with their axons form the pyramidal tracts descending in the brainstem and spinal cord. VI. The polymorphic layer (multiform layer) (VI): It is the deepest and broadest layer in the cortex. The cells of this layer have variable sizes and shapes (fusiform, triangular and ovoid). Cytoarchitecture of some cerebral areas: 1- Motor area (precentral gyrus): • It is Agranular type:  Few granule cells.  Well developed pyramidal cell layers (Betz cells in the internal pyramidal layer). 2- Sensory area (post central gyrus): • It is Granular type:  Well developed granular layers.  Ill defined pyramidal layers(few & small pyramidal cells)

text: Synaptic plasticity-Memory Synaptic plasticity: is the ability of synapses to strengthen or weaken over time, in response to increases or decreases in their activity . Remodelling of synaptic structures occurs throughout a lifetime and maximally during development. Synaptic plasticity could be in the form of synaptic depression or synaptic facilitation. Synaptic plasticity plays important roles in different forms of learning and memory. Memory is power to retain and recall information and past experiences. The neural change responsible for retention or storage of knowledge is known as the memory trace. Generally, concepts, not literal information, are stored. As you read this page, you are storing the concept discussed, not the specific words. Later, when you r etrieve the concept from memory, you will convert it into your own words. It is possible, however, to memorize bits of information word by word. Storage of acquired information is accomplished in at least two stages: short -term memory and long-term memory . Short-term memory lasts for seconds to hours, whereas long-term memory is retained for days to years. The process of transferring and fixing short -term memory traces into long- term memory stores is known as consolidation. (Table-1) According to the type of stored information, memory can be divided into two types: 1. Declarative memory (Explicit) is acquiring new facts about the world. This leads to the formation of two types of memory—episodic memory (remembering events such as last year’s holiday), and semantic memory (remembering facts such as 'Paris is the capital of France', ). 2. Procedural (motor)-non declarative memory -Implicit They include the memories for skills and habits (e.g., riding a bicycle, driving a car, playing tennis or a piano) Declarative learning is relatively easy to acquire; many memories only need a single exposure. They require conscious recall and may be forgotten. In contrast, procedural learning is slow, in that for many skills, repeated practice is required. Its recall is unconscious and it is not easily lost Working memory, Working memory temporarily holds various pieces of information relevant to a current mental task. Through your working memory, you briefly hold and process data for immediate use—both newly acquired information and related, previously stored knowledge that is transiently brought forth into working memory —so that you can evaluate the incoming data in context. This integrative function is crucial to your ability to reason, plan, and make judgments. By comparing and manipulating new and old information within your working memory, you can comprehend what you are reading, carry on a conversation, calculate a restaurant tip in your head, find your way home, and know that you should put on warm clothing if you see snow outside. Working memory is regulated by the prefrontal association cortex. The prefrontal cortex serves as a temporary storage site for holdin g relevant data and is largely responsible for the so -called executive functions involving manipulation and integration of this information for planning, problem solving, and organizing activities. Mechanisms of Short-term and long-term memory Different mechanisms are responsible for short -term and long -term memory. Short -term memory involves transient modifications in the function of preexisting synapses , such as a Table-1 temporary change in the amount of neurotransmitter released in response to stimulation or temporarily increased responsiveness of the postsynaptic cell to the neurotransmitter within affected nerve pathways. Long -term memory, in contrast, involves relatively permanent functional or structural changes between existing neurons in the brain. Whereas short -term memory involves transient strengthening of preexisting synapses, long -term memory storage requires the activation of specific genes that control synthesis of proteins needed for lasting structural or functional changes at specific synapses. Examples of such changes include the formation of new synaptic connections or permanent change s in pre -or postsynaptic membranes. Brain areas responsible for memory storage There is no single “memory center” in the brain , however, the neurons involved in memory traces are widely distributed throughout the subcortical and cortical regions of the br ain. The regions of the brain most extensively implicated in memory include the HIPPOCAMPUS and associated structures of the medial temporal lobes, the limbic system, the cerebellum, the prefrontal cortex, and other areas of the cerebral cortex. THE CEREBELLUM AND PROCEDURAL MEMORIES The cerebellum and relevant cortical regions play an essential role in the “how to” procedural memories involving motor skills gained through repetitive training, such as memorizing a particular skill routine. The cortical areas important for a given procedural memory are the specific motor or sensory systems engaged in performing the routine. In contrast to declarative memories, which are consciously recollected from previous experiences, procedural memories can be brought forth without conscious effort. For example, an ice skater during a competition typically performs best by “letting the body take over” t he routine instead of thinking about exactly what needs to be done next. The two forms of non-declarative memory—habituation and sensitization —are due to modification of different channel proteins in presynaptic terminals of specific afferent neurons involved in the pathway that mediates the behavior being modified. This modification, in turn, brings about changes in transmitter release. HABITUATION is a decreased responsiveness to repetitive presentations of an indifferent stimulus —that is, one that is ne ither rewarding nor punishing. SENSITIZATION is increased responsiveness to mild stimuli following a strong or noxious stimulus. MECHANISM OF HABITUATION : Recall that when an action potential arrives in a presynaptic axon terminal, voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open, permitting the entry of Ca2+ that triggers the exocytosis of neurotransmitter. As a result of habituation, these Ca 2+ channels do not open as readily when an action potential arrives, reducing Ca 2+ entry into the presynapt ic terminal, which leads to a decrease in neurotransmitter release. As a consequence, the postsynaptic potential is reduced compared to normal, resulting in a decrease or absence of the behavioral response controlled by the postsynaptic efferent neuron. (Fig. 1) MECHANISM OF SENSITIZATION : In contrast to what happens in habituation, Ca2+ entry into the presynaptic terminal is enhanced in sensitization. The subsequent increase in neurotransmitter release produces a larger postsynaptic potential, resulting in a more strong response. Sensitization does not have a direct effect on presynaptic Ca2+ channels. Instead, it indirectly enhances Ca2+ entry via presynaptic facilitation. The neurotransmitter serotonin is released from a facilitating interneuron that synapses on the presynaptic terminal to bring about increased release of presynaptic neurotransmitter in response to an action potential. It does so by blocking of K+ channels. This blockage prolongs the action potential in the presynaptic terminal. A prolonged action poten tial permits the greater Ca2+ influx associated with sensitization. (Fig.2) Thus, existing synaptic pathways may be functionally interrupted (habituated) or enhanced (sensitized) during simple learning. Fig. 1 Fig. 2 Involvement of the hippocampus in memory formation Hippocampus is the medial portion of the temporal lobe and is a part of the limbic system . Hippocampus is central in the consolidation of newly acquired memories, particularly declarative memory. Long term potentiation (LTP) is especially prevalent in the hippocampus and is critical for converting short-term memories into long-term memories. (Fig. 3: mechanism of LTP) Fig. 3 Mechanism of LTP.Note that LTP develops in response to frequent activity across a synapse as a result of repetitive, intense firing of a given input (as with repeatedly going over a particular fact during studying) or to the linking of one input with another input firing at the same time. Therefore, After the input pathway is strengthened through development of LTP and ultimate consolidation into long-term storage. Amnesia Memory loss occurs in two ways. Loss of recent memory, including the inability to form new memories, is ANTERO- GRADE AMNESIA , and suggests that there is a defect in the memory storage process. A failure in recall leads to the inability to retrieve previously stored memories, producing RETRO-GRADE AMNESIA. This type of amnesia may be progressive, with mor e recent memories being lost first. Dementia is a term that describes a progressive and irreversible loss of higher mental function, particu- larly memory. Cognitive decline is associated with alterations in mood and behaviour that lead to complete disintegration of the personality .Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia and may contribute to 60-70% of cases. text: L26: Effects of lesion to descending tracts at different levels Transfer goal To correlate the functions and organization of the descending tracts to the lesions that might occur. ILOs 1. Describe clinical signs of different upper and lower motor neuron lesions and explain their pathophysiology. 2. Compare between such neuron lesions 3. Interpret clinical Scenarios based on understanding of different lesions Recap Motor neuron lesions Upper motor neuron lesion (UMNL) Lower motor neuron lesion (LMNL) Functional anatomy of the spinal cord Upper motor neuron lesion (UMNL) lesions which affect the cortical motor areas or the pathways of the descending tracts in the brain or spinal cord. Causes: Mainly vascular. Trauma Tumor Degenerative diseases. The most common lesions are lesions of the internal capsule commonly caused by vascular disorders. Manifestations of UMNL Paralysis: - Opposite side (due to crossing of the motor tract) - Widespread (pyramidal fibers form a compact bundle which occupies a small area) Manifestations of UMNL 2. Spasticity (increased muscle tone): Decrease of the inhibitory discharge (from the IRF) on the gamma efferent while the facilitatory discharge continues ( from the FRF) Cause of spasticity: Normally the facilitatory reticular formation discharges spontaneously, possibly in response to afferent input like the reticular activating system. The inhibitory reticular formation does not discharge spontaneously but is driven instead by fibers from the cerebral cortex. In UMNL there is interruption of the cortical discharge to the inhibitory reticular formation which decreases its activity. Hence the balance between inhibition and facilitation shifts towards facilitation and the gamma efferent discharge is increased. Furthermore the vestibulospinal tracts remain intact and they also have a facilitatory effect on muscle tone. Manifestations of UMNL 3. Increased (exaggerated) deep reflexes and may be clonus Due to state of supraspinal facilitation that increases the activity of muscle spindle to stretch. Manifestations of UMNL 4. clonus Alternating regular rhythmic contractions and relaxations of a of spastic paralyzed muscle in response to sudden sustained stretch. Mechanism of clonus: Clonus is the result of a stretch reflex - inverse stretch reflex sequence. Sudden stretch of the muscle (nuclear bag) Its contraction through the stretch reflex. Stimulation of the GTOs Initiation of an inverse stretch reflex Relaxation As stretch is maintained a new stretch reflex occurs (helped by the state of excessive spinal facilitation). Manifestations of UMNL 5. Superficial reflexes Superficial reflexes as abdominal and withdrawal reflexes are lost because superficial reflexes receive facilitatory influence from the pyramidal tract. Upper motor neuron lesion (UMNL) Manifestations: 1 - Paralysis: 2. Spasticity (increased muscle tone): 3 - Increased (exaggerated) deep reflexes and may be clonus. 4- Superficial reflexes. 5- Plantar reflex Extensor plantar responses (positive Babinski sign) Babinski sign is a part of the spinal withdrawal reflex which in normal subject is inhibited by the corticospinal tract. Plantar reflex Manifestations: 1 - Paralysis: 2. Spasticity (increased muscle tone): 3 - Increased (exaggerated) deep reflexes and may be clonus. 4- Superficial reflexes. 5- Plantar reflex. 6 - Muscle status There is no or little wasting. Upper motor neuron lesion (UMNL) Lower motor neuron lesion (LMNL) Lower motor neuron lesion (LMNL) Definition: Lower motor neuron lesion (LMNL) means lesion or damage to the lower motor neurons in the spinal ventral horns (or motor nerve or damage to the muscle) or the corresponding motor nuclei of cranial nerves in the brain stem. Causes: Mainly poliomyelitis or trauma to peripheral nerves. Manifestations: Paralysis: On the same side and localized. Decreased tone (hypotonia) or flaccidity due to cut of stretch reflex arc. Decreased or (absent) deep reflexes in the affected segment. Plantar reflex: either normal or absent if the involved muscles are paralyzed. Superficial reflexes: Lost in the affected segment (if they involve contraction of the denervated muscle). Muscle status: There is marked wasting because the muscle is deprived of its motor supply. N.B. signs of muscle denervation could be elicited as fasciculation (muscle twitches visible under the skin due to denervation of motor units)and fibrillations (muscles potentials detected by electromyography in denervated muscles). Lower motor neuron lesion (LMNL) Spinal cord injury (SCI) Trauma injuries are often the most common and can be caused directly by penetrating injuries such as gun Shot or stab wounds, or indirectly as a result of compression or flexion/extension injuries of structures associated with the vertebral column. This can lead to sensory, motor or sphincter dysfunction or a combination of these, depending on whether the lesion is uni- or bilateral. SCI can either be: COMPLETE: meaning that there is no voluntary movement or sensation below the level of the lesion on both sides, INCOMPLETE: when there is a variable amount of function below the level of the lesion. Manifestations of SCI One of the earliest signs of SCI is pain. Motor dysfunction also occurs early, resulting in hypotonia, muscle wasting and paralysis. Depending on the level of the lesion, there may bn cardiovascular, respiratory and autonomic (bladder, sweating and sexual) function, as well as a loss of protective functions such as pain and temperature I. Complete transection of the spinal cord causes: Trauma. Tumour. Ischemia Demyelinating diseases. According to the level of lesion: Above the level of C3, breathing could be affected. Lower cervical region results in quadriplegia i.e. paralysis of the four limbs. Thoracic region results in paraplegia i.e. paralysis of both lower limbs. Spinal shock : When the transection is complete there is usually a period after the accident when all spinal reflexes below the level of the transection are REDUCED .This condition is known as spinal shock. Stage of recovery During the course of weeks and months spinal reflexes GRADUALLY RETURN, often greatly exaggerated compared with normal which is described as stage of recovery. If complications are present the duration of spinal shock is much longer or even failure of recovery occurs. Complication could be urinary tract infection, malnutrition and decubitus ulcers. Therefore, adequate management of the paraplegic patient is very important to prevent occurrence of complications I. Complete transection of the spinal cord Stage of spinal shock Manifestations: 1. Loss of all sensations. 2. Loss of all voluntary movements below the level of the lesion. 3. Loss of cord reflexes as stretch reflex and flexor withdrawal reflex etc… 4. loss of Bladder and bowl control (retention with overflow) 5. Loss of erection 6. Drop of the arterial blood pressure if the transection is at the level of first thoracic segment, but slight drop occurs if the lesion is below the second lumber segment, due to block of the sympathetic activity. Autonomic Motor Sensory Duration: The duration of spinal shock is much shorter in animals than in human (in animals it lasts for minutes up to hours or day). The long recovery period for humans reflects the greater influence of descending input on spinal reflex circuits. Cause: Spinal shock is due to sudden withdrawal of tonic facilitatory influence from the brain Stage of spinal shock N.B The spinal cord ends at the level of the base of the second lumbar vertebra. Below this level the spinal canal is occupied by the lower nerve roots. Therefore, injuries to the spinal canal below vertebral level L2 cause sensory loss in the region of the body innervated by the lower lumbar and sacral nerve roots as well as a lower motor neuron weakness and decreased tendon reflexes in certain leg muscles. 27 Stage of recovery Manifestations: 1. Recovery of spinal reflexes as stretch reflex, they are often exaggerated compared with normal. 2. The spinal sympathetic vasoconstrictor centers in the lateral horn below the level of the transection regain their activity and send their impulses to the arterioles and veins, which regain tone. 3. Micturition and defecation become automatic as in children with residual urine due to weakness of the reflex. 4. Touch of the patient with a noxious stimulus applied to the skin produces a flexor withdrawal reflex and impulses may irradiate to autonomic centers which lead to provocation of a mass reflex 28 Mass reflex Stimulus: Touch of the patient with a noxious stimulus applied to the skin. Response: Flexor withdrawal reflex wide spreading flexor activity as flexor spasm of both lower extremities and contraction of the anterior abdominal wall. Impulses may irradiate to autonomic centers i.e. sweating, pallor, swinging blood pressure, micturition, defecation. Mechanism: It presumably results from activation of great number of neuronal circuits that excite large areas of the cord at once ; it is similar to the mechanism of epileptic fits that involve circuits in the brain instead of the cord. Stage of recovery Mechanism: Several mechanisms may contribute to recovery: Denervation hypersensitivity to the mediators released by the remaining spinal excitatory endings. Increased number of postsynaptic receptors and the sprouting of collaterals. Increase number of receptors Decrease uptake of secreted NT Collaterals sprouts are new branches formed by other non damaged axons that attach to vacant receptors. Cells that have lost their source of innervation release neurotrophins that induce axons to form collateral sprouts. 30 Stage of recovery Manifestations: 1. Recovery of spinal reflexes 2. Recovery of sympathetic vasoconstrictor 3. Micturition and defecation become automatic 4. Mass reflex Mechanism: Several mechanisms may contribute to recovery: Denervation hypersensitivity to the mediators released by the remaining spinal excitatory endings. Increased number of postsynaptic receptors and the sprouting of collaterals. Spinal shock Recovery Duration 2-6 weeks Variable weeks-months Cause Sudden withdrawal of supraspinal facilitation (continuous tonic discharge).on the alpha motor neurons (coming from reticulospinal, vestibulospinal and cortoicpspinal tracts) Increase in degree of excitability of the spinal cord neurons below the level of the lesion due to: Disinhbition of motor neurons due to absence of inhibitory impulses from higher motor centers. Deneravtion sensitivity Sprouting of collaterals Manifestation Paralysis of all muscles. BELOW the lesion (UMNL) Loss of all sensations BELOW the lesion. Loss of all deep and superficial reflexes. Flaccidity Retention with overflow Vasodilatation (due to loss of vasomotor tone)—hypotension Gradual increase in blood pressure Return of spinal reflexes: Stretch reflex Babinski sign Flexor tendon reflexes Automatic micturition Mass reflex Voluntary movements and sensations are permanently lost If one side of the cord is transected leads to characteristic pattern known as Brown Sequard syndrome caused commonly by: Penetrating trauma. Ruptured disk Hemisection of the spinal cord 33 Hemisection of the spinal cord Charles-Édouard Brown-Séquard (April 8, 1817 - April 2, 1894), also known as Charles Edward, was a physiologist and neurologist. He contributed largely to our knowledge of the highest importance on the nervous system. - He was the first scientist to work out the physiology of the spinal cord, demonstrating that the decussation of the fibers carrying pain and temperature sensation occurs in the cord itself. He was the first to describe the syndrome which bears his name, Brown-Séquard syndrome, a loss of sensation and motor function (paralysis and ataxia) that is caused by the lateral hemisection (cutting) of the spinal cord. 35 Ipsilateral: 1. Motor paralysis (corticospinal) 2. Fine touch (dorsal column) Contralateral: 1. Pain & temp. (spinothalamic) Below the hemisection: On the same side (ipsilateral): 1. Paralysis of voluntary movements due to interruption of the descending motor pathways (UMNL). 2. Loss of dorsal column sensations (vibration sense, tactile discrimination and light touch). However, the spino-thalamic sensations are preserved. On the opposite side (contralateral): sensation of pain and temperature are lost due to cut of lateral spinothalamic tract coming from the intact side. At the level of hemisection 1. LMN paralysis of muscles supplied by the damaged segment ( no voluntary or reflex action) 2. loss of all sensations (superficial and deep) from areas supplied by the dorsal roots entering the cord in the damaged segments. Above the level of the lesion: On the same side ( one or two segments) Cutaneous hypersthesia Due to irritation of dorsal nerve roots by the neighboring lesion. Syringomyelia What is syringomelia? Syringomyelia is a developmental abnormality. Results in a cavity formation in the spinal cord originating in the central canal. It is common at the cervical spinal cord. Manifestations: The cavity interrupts the crossing spinothalamic fibers leading to bilateral loss of pain, and temperature sensations at level of affected segments. The dorsal column sensation of same segments remain intact. syringomyelia is an example of dissociated anesthesia. Syringomyelia - In late stages, the overgrowing tissue extends towards the ventral spinal horn destroying the anterior horn cells producing muscle weakness and may be muscle atrophy at the level of affected segment. Decorticate and decerebrate rigidity When physical or vascular damage to the brainstem produces functional disconnection between the red nucleus (midbrain) and the vestibular nuclei (pons), patients show an increase in extensor muscle tone, called decerebrate rigidity. Cause: It is caused by tonic activity in the lateral vestibulo- spinal and reticulospinal tracts that act on the extensor motor neurones, and the loss of rubrospinal inhibition of extensor motor neurons. CLINICAL APPLICATION Polio and post polio syndrome Infection with the polio virus results in several different body responses. Most cases are asymptomatic. There are two other forms: Non-paralytic ; which produce transient (2–10 )days with complete recovery paralytic polio; permanent muscle weakness and paralysis.patients suffer flaccid paralysis of muscles and painful spasms in non-paralysed muscles. The amount of paralysis is inversely proportional to the motor neurone loss. CLINICAL APPLICATION The virus enters through the mouth ------ >bloodstream to ---🡪 central nervous system motor targets, such as the cerebellum, vestibular system, motor cortex and reticular formation. It can travel along peripheral nerves to infect lower motor neurones. Polio occurs most often in children. The affected muscles become atrophied and the limb is flaccid and small. Nowadays, in the western hemisphere, polio has been eradicated by a WHO vaccination programme. Children receive three oral polio vaccinations of a live attenuated version of the virus to enable them to develop antibodies to the virus. LMNL Page 172-174

Chimeric figures test The white matter of the brain is divided into: Association fibers Commissural fibers Projection fibers Association fibers: Connect 2 areas on the same side of the cerebral hemisphere, includes: A. Short association fibers : connecting adjacent gyri together. B. Long association fibers Association fibers II. Commissural fibers: These connect between 2 same areas on both sides of the cerebral hemispheres. Commissural fibers The brain houses two minds, not one, but they only orchestrate into a single personality if the two cerebral hemispheres communicate& exchange information, as by the commissural fibers. Thus, consciousness is controlled by both hemispheres, and there is crossing over of functions so that one never normally experiences a dissociation of information. Commissural Fibers: Commissural Fibers: Anterior commissure: It connects between olfactory structures of both sides (olfactory bulb; anterior perforated substance). 2. Posterior commissure: it is present just above the upper end of the cerebral aqueduct. it connects between visual structures on both sides Commissural Fibers: 3. Hippocampal commissure (or commissure of the fornix): These fibers connect the hippocampus with its fellow of the opposite side. Commissural Fibers: It is the greatest commissure. It is divided into: Rostrum, is the thin part of the anterior end of the corpus callosum, Genu, the curved anterior end of the corpus callosum, Body, arches posteriorly and ends as the splenium Splenium. 4. Corpus callosum: Commissural Fibers: Rostrum: Connects between the orbital surface of the frontal lobes on both sides. Genu: Connects the anterior part of the frontal lobes on both sides. The fibers of the genu radiate forwards towards the frontal poles forming the forceps minor. Body: Connects between the posterior part of the frontal lobe and anterior part of the parietal lobe on both sides. Splenium: Connects between the posterior part of the parietal lobe, temporal lobe and occipital lobe on both sides. These fibers pass either: Lateral to the posterior horn of the lateral ventricle and are called tapetum. Medial to the posterior horn of the lateral ventricle and are called forceps major. Corpus callosum: ‘Split-brain’ syndrome ‘Splitting’ the brain, by sectioning the corpus callosum, and thereby disconnecting the hemispheres, was used by surgeons to treat chronic intractable forms of epilepsy. To the casual observer, the split-brain patients appeared normal and their seizures disappeared. However, psychological testing revealed that if the patient held up an object like a comb in the left hand, they could not say what it was. When it was transferred to the right hand, the patient had no trouble at all to identity it . The same happened with words. If a card with a printed word like ‘ring’ was visible only in the patient’s left visual field, they could not read it, yet vision in the left eye was fine. When the word was in the right field, the patient immediately recognized it. III. Projection fibers: These are fibers passing from or to the cerebral cortex; thus they are subdivided into: Ascending fibers B. Descending fibers e.g. for the projection fibers is the Internal Capsule INTERNAL CAPSULE The internal capsule is composed of all the fibers, afferent and efferent, which go to, or come from, the cerebral cortex. A. Anterior limb: Frontopontine fibers. Anterior thalamic radiation. B. Genu: Corticobulbar fibers. C. Posterior limb: Subdivided into: Thalamolentiform part: Lies between the lentiform nucleus and the thalamus; contains: Parietopontine fibers. Superior thalamic radiation Corticospinal tract. Corticorubral. 5. Corticostriate. Fibers of the internal capsule II. Retrolentifrom part: Extends caudally behind the lentiform nucleus; contains: 1. Occipitopontine fibers. 2. Posterior thalamic radiation including optic radiation. III. Sublentifrom part: Passing beneath the lentiform nucleus; contains: 1. Tempropontine fibers. 2. Inferior thalamic radiation including auditory radiation. Fibers of the internal capsule Both anterior and posterior limbs are supplied primarily by branches of the middle cerebral artery. In addition , each part of the internal capsule receives another arterial branch: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the anteromedial parts of the anterior limb. The genu receives direct branches from the internal carotid artery. The ventral portion of the posterior limb and its entire retrolenticular part are supplied by branches of the anterior choroid artery. Demyelinating disorders These are acquired conditions characterized by preferential damage to Myelin with relative preservation of axons. 5 Etiology\pathogenesis of demyelinating disorders Vitamin B12 Copper deficiency Hypoxia, medications and toxins Impaired memory Cognitive alterations Visual problems Abnormal behavior Brain Sensory changes Motor weakness Reduced bowel or urinary control Spinal cord\spinal nerves Stoke and gloves peripheral neuropathy Peripheral nerves Clinical effects of demyelination Depends on the affected area of the nervous system. History and outcomes of demyelination are determined by; - The limited capacity of the CNS to regenerate normal myelin - The degree of secondary damage to axons that occurs as the disease runs its course. An autoimmune demyelinating disorder characterized by distinct episodes of neurologic deficits that are separated in time and are attributable to patchy white matter lesions that are separated in space. Multiple sclerosis (MS) Pathogenesis of MS 1- Genetic predisposition Antigen-antibody Pathogenesis of MS 2- Autoimmunity → cytokines → inflammation → destruction of myelin → loss of function with axon preservation) → LATELY, undergo at some point axonal damage and neurodegeneration. 11 Multifocal large "plaques" of demyelination in the white matter , in a predominantly periventricular location. text: 1 TU 1 Nutritional Needs for Proper Neuronal Function ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Recognize micro and macro nutrients of importance for proper neuronal function 2. Identify sources and body requirements of such nutrients 3. Highlight metabolism of some micronutrients of importance 4. Correlate deficiencies and toxicity of such nutrients to clinical conditions Many micronutrients (vitamins and minerals) and macronutrients (carbohydrates, lipids and proteins) play an important role in proper neural function Micronutrients of importance in nervous system 1) Folic acid (Vitamin B9) Folic acid (or folate), which plays a key role in one-carbon metabolism, is essential for the biosynthesis of several compounds. Folic acid deficiency is probably one of the most common vitamin deficiencies, particularly among pregnant women and individuals with alcoholism. Dietary sources Leafy, dark green vegetables are a good source of folic acid. Function Tetrahydrofolate (THF), the reduced, coenzyme form of folate, receives one-carbon fragments from donors such as serine, glycine, and histidine and transfers them to intermediates in the synthesis of amino acids, purine nucleotides, and thymidine monophosphate (TMP), a pyrimidine nucleotide incorporated into DNA (Fig. 1) Figure 1: Metabolism of 1 carbon moieties by Folic acid 2 Folate deficiency presents as: 1- Megaloblastic anemia because of decreased availability of the purines and of the thymidine monophosphate needed for DNA synthesis, thus the blood cells are immature and larger than usual. 2-Neural tube defects: Spina bifida and anencephaly are the most common neural tube defects (NTD). Folic acid supplementation before conception and during the first trimester has been shown to significantly reduce NTD. Therefore, all women of childbearing age are advised to consume 0.4 mg/day (400 μg/day) of folic acid to reduce the risk of having a pregnancy affected by NTD and ten times that amount if a previous pregnancy was affected. 2-Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin) Structure and coenzyme forms (Figure 2)  Cobalamin contains a corrin ring system that resembles the porphyrin ring of heme .  Cobalt is held in the center of the corrin ring by four coordination bonds with the nitrogens of the pyrrole groups.  The remaining coordination bonds of the cobalt are with the nitrogen of 5,6-dimethyl-benz- imidazole and with cyanide in commercial preparations of the vitamin in the form of cyanocobalamin. The physiologic coenzyme forms of cobalamin are 5′- deoxyadenosylcobalamin and methylcobalamin, in which cyanide is replaced with 5′- deoxyadenosine or a methyl group, respectively Figure 2: Structure and coenzymes forms of vit.B12 Dietary sources Vitamin B12 is synthesized only by microorganisms, and it is not present in plants. Animals obtain the vitamin preformed from their intestinal microbiota or by eating foods derived from 3 other animals. Cobalamin is present in appreciable amounts in liver, red meat, fish, eggs, dairy products, and fortified cereals. Functions Vitamin B12 is required in humans for two essential enzymatic reactions: 1) Remethylation of homocysteine (Hcy) to methionine [Note: Folic acid (as N5-methyl THF) is also required in the remethylation of Hcy. Therefore, deficiency of B12 or folate results in elevated Hcy levels.] (Fig. 3). 2) Isomerization of methylmalonyl coenzyme A (CoA), which is produced during the degradation of some amino acids (isoleucine, valine, threonine, and methionine) and fatty acids (FA) with odd numbers of carbon atoms (Fig. 4). Figure 3 Absorption of B12 (Figure 5)  B12 is released from food in the acidic environment of the stomach. Free B12 then binds a glycoprotein (R-protein or haptocorrin), and the complex moves into the intestine.  B12 is released from the R-protein by pancreatic enzymes and binds another glycoprotein, intrinsic factor (IF).  The cobalamin–IF complex travels through the intestine and binds to a receptor (cubilin) on the surface of mucosal cells in the ileum.  The cobalamin is transported into the mucosal cell and, subsequently, into the general circulation, where it is carried by its binding protein (transcobalamin). Figure 4 4  B12 is taken up and stored in the liver, primarily. It is released into bile and efficiently reabsorbed in the ileum. Severe malabsorption of vitamin B12 leads to pernicious anemia. Vit B12 Deficiency  In contrast to other water-soluble vitamins, significant amounts (2–5 mg) of vitamin B12 are stored in the body. As a result, it may take several years for the clinical symptoms of B12 deficiency to develop as a result of decreased intake of the vitamin. [Note: Deficiency happens much more quickly (in months) if absorption is impaired.  The Schilling test evaluates B12 absorption. B12 deficiency can be determined by the level of methylmalonic acid in blood, which is elevated in individuals with low intake or decreased absorption of the vitamin. B12 deficiency:  Vitamin B12 deficiency is most commonly seen in patients who fail to absorb the vitamin from the intestine .. [Note: Malabsorption of cobalamin in the elderly is most often due to reduced secretion of gastric acid (achlorhydria).  This disease is most commonly a result of an autoimmune destruction of the gastric parietal cells that are responsible for the synthesis of IF (lack of IF prevents B12 absorption).  Patients who have had a partial or total gastrectomy become IF deficient and, therefore, B12 deficient. Manifestations of vit B12 deficiency 1- subacute combined cord degeneration. The most common neurological presentation of vit B12 deficiency is 2- Pernicious anemia:  Usually due to an autoimmune disease resulting in achlorohydria and deficiency of intrinsic factor thus impairing vit B12 absorption. Individuals with pernicious anemia usually suffer from megaloblastic anemia (folate recycling is impaired, see below), and they show neuropsychiatric symptoms as the disease develops.  Neurological symptoms are due to accumulation and incorporation of unusual (branched) fatty acid into cell membranes, including those of the central nervous system, thus affecting proper neural transmission. Another reason for neurological manifestations is accumulation of methyl malonic acid and homocysteine which are neurotoxic. Figure 5: Absorption of vit B12 5  Pernicious anemia requires lifelong treatment with either high-dose oral B12 or intramuscular injection of cyanocobalamin. [Note: Supplementation works even in the absence of IF because ~1% of B12 uptake is by IF-independent diffusion.] Folate trap hypothesis  The effects of cobalamin deficiency are most pronounced in rapidly dividing cells, such as the erythropoietic tissue of bone marrow and the mucosal cells of the intestine.  Such tissues need both the N5,N10-methylene and N10-formyl forms of THF for the synthesis of nucleotides required for DNA replication (see fig.1). However, in vitamin B12 deficiency, the utilization of the N5-methyl form of THF in the B12- dependent methylation of Hcy to methionine is impaired.  Because the methylated form cannot be converted directly to other forms of THF, folate is trapped in the N5-methyl form, which accumulates. The levels of the other forms decrease. Thus, cobalamin deficiency leads to a deficiency of the THF forms needed in purine and TMP synthesis, resulting in the symptoms of megaloblastic anemia. Treatment of B12 deficiency Folic acid supplementation can partially reverse the hematologic abnormalities of B12 deficiency and, therefore, can mask a cobalamin deficiency. Thus, to prevent the later CNS effects of B12 deficiency, therapy for megaloblastic anemia is initiated with both vitamin B12 and folic acid until the cause of the anemia can be determined. Vit B6 Vitamin B6 is a water soluble vitamin that acts as a coenzyme in the process of synthesis of several neurotransmitters from aminoacids by decarboxylation, for example GABA from glutamate and histamine from histidine. B6 deficiency can lead to peripheral neuropathy. FIGLU test: Formiminoglutamic acid (FIGLU) is an intermediate metabolite in L-histidine catabolism in the conversion of L-histidine to L-glutamic acid. If urinary FIGLU is increased, it may be an indicator of vitamin B12 or folic acid deficiency or liver disease. Other clinical conditions leading to increased FIGLU include alcohol consumption, pregnancy, and birth control use. To differentiate between isolated B12 deficiency and folate deficiency, methylmalonate will be elevated in the urine only in cases of vitamin B12 deficiency Wernick’s korsakoff syndrome: A form of irreversible memory loss due to vitamin B1 deficiency. Usually occurs due to alcoholism A popular treatment for peripheral neuritis is an injection of combined vit B1, B6 and B12 6 Macronutrients on importance in neural function Sphingophospholipids: Sphingomyelin  The backbone of sphingomyelin is the amino alcohol sphingosine, rather than glycerol . A long-chain-length FA (LCFA) is attached to the amino group of sphingosine through an amide linkage, producing a ceramide, which can also serve as a precursor of glycolipids.  The alcohol group at carbon 1 of sphingosine is esterified to phosphorylcholine, producing sphingomyelin, the only significant sphingophospholipid in humans. Sphingomyelin is an important constituent of the myelin sheath of nerve fibers Sphingolipidoses  In a normal individual, synthesis and degradation of glycosphingolipids are balanced, so that the amount of these compounds present in membranes is constant. If a specific lysosomal acid hydrolase required for degradation is partially or totally missing, a sphingolipid accumulates. Lysosomal lipid storage diseases caused by these deficiencies are called sphingolipidoses.  The result of a specific acid hydrolase deficiency may be seen dramatically in nerve tissue, where neurologic deterioration can lead mental retardation and early death. Liver of such patients is usually enlarged due to accumulation of lipid droplets.  Sphingolipidosis contains several diseases. The incidence of the sphingolipidoses is low in most populations, except for Gaucher and Tay-Sachs diseases, which, like Niemann-Pick disease, show a high frequency in the Ashkenazi Jewish population.Most of such diseases are autosomal-recessive disorders, except for Fabry disease, which is X linked.
